editorial.headline: Motorcycle Parts Retail: Open Nationally, Barred to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: Retailing new or used motorcycle parts and accessories is nationally open to PMA, yet Bali’s permanent risk-based moratorium blocks PMA registration for this activity.
editorial.body:
KBLI 47833 covers the retail trade in motorcycle parts and accessories, whether new or used. It concerns the retail point at which replacement components and add-ons meet the customer, with the record also placing the activity alongside direct sales. The definition is deliberately product-specific: motorcycle parts and accessories, rather than a broad description of every commercial activity connected with motorcycles. Its scope expressly extends to both new and used stock, keeping the activity anchored to the retail sale of those goods.

Registration is open at every scale named in the record: Micro, Small, Medium and Large. That breadth does not make the classification a catch-all business description; it means the stated retail activity may be undertaken across those business scales. For a founder, the practical starting point is to keep the operating description precise: retail sale of motorcycle parts and accessories, new or used. The national investment position is equally direct. The activity is open to PMA, with a national foreign-ownership ceiling of 100% under the cited Presidential Regulations.

That national opening does not carry through to Bali. In Bali today, a foreign investor cannot register this activity as PMA. The Bali record marks it as blocked by risk class: at the Large scale, OSS assigns Low or Medium-Low risk across every scope. Bali’s island-wide, permanent moratorium blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI from PMA registration. The stated moratorium date is May 2026, and the result for this activity is not a softer local preference or a reduced foreign-ownership allowance: it is a registration block for PMA in Bali.

The distinction calls for an exact reading. Nationally, the code is open to foreign investment up to 100%; in Bali, its relevant risk classification brings it within an island-wide PMA prohibition. Both propositions come from the same record and must be held together rather than collapsed into a single claim of openness. A business may fit the retail scope and be available across every listed scale at the national level, yet that does not change the Bali registration outcome for a PMA applicant. For decisions involving Bali, the blocked status is the decisive fact.
editorial.pullQuote: Nationally open to 100% foreign ownership, this activity is nevertheless blocked from PMA registration in Bali.
